problems.title: T beam bending stress
problems.setup: A T beam has a flange 80 mm wide × 20 mm thick on top of a web 20 mm thick × 120 mm deep (total depth 140 mm). It carries a sagging bending moment M = 10 kN·m about the horizontal centroidal axis. Measure y upward from the bottom of the web; the material is linear elastic.

parts.ask: Height of the centroid above the bottom of the web
sol: Flange: A = 1600 mm², y = 130 mm; web: A = 2400 mm², y = 60 mm

parts.ask: Second moment of area about the centroidal axis, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴ (ȳ = 88 mm)
sol: I = 7.637e6 mm⁴ by the parallel axis theorem

parts.ask: Maximum tensile bending stress (I = 7.637×10⁶ mm⁴)
sol: Sagging puts the bottom fiber in tension, c = 88 mm

parts.ask: The same beam now carries a hogging moment of 10 kN·m. Where is the largest tensile stress and its value?
sol: Hogging puts the top in tension, c = 140 − 88 = 52 mm
σ = 10e6·52/7.637e6 = 68.1 MPa, while the bottom carries 115.2 MPa compression

problems.x: The centroid sits near the wide flange, so the fiber farthest from it (the web tip) carries the largest bending stress.

problems.title: Unsymmetric section principal axes
problems.setup: A thin angle section has centroidal properties I_y = 4×10⁶ mm⁴, I_z = 2×10⁶ mm⁴ and product I_yz = 1×10⁶ mm⁴. A bending moment M = 5 kN·m is applied about principal axis 1 (the axis of the larger principal moment). Point Q lies 50 mm from principal axis 1, measured along principal axis 2.

parts.ask: Larger principal second moment I₁, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴
Magnitude of the angle between the y axis and principal axis 1
Bending stress magnitude at Q (I₁ = 4.414×10⁶ mm⁴)
sol: About a principal axis the flexure formula uncouples: σ = M·d/I₁

parts.ask: If the same moment acts about the centroidal y axis instead, the neutral axis:
parts.a: Is inclined to the y axis
w: Passes through the shear centre only
Is parallel to the z axis
sol: With I_yz ≠ 0 a moment about y produces curvature about both y and z
The neutral axis rotates away from the moment axis and the beam deflects out of the load plane

problems.x: Resolve the moment onto principal axes, where the simple flexure formula applies to each component separately.

problems.title: Channel shear flow and shear centre
problems.setup: A thin channel has web height h = 200 mm and two flanges of width b = 100 mm, all with wall thickness t = 2 mm (dimensions to the wall midlines). It carries a vertical shear force V = 10 kN. Neglect the flanges' own second moment about their midlines.

parts.ask: Second moment of area I about the horizontal centroidal axis, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴
Shear flow at the flange to web corner
Maximum shear stress in the web (at the neutral axis)
Shear centre location measured from the web midline
parts.a: 37.5 mm, on the side away from the flanges
w: 37.5 mm, between the web and the flange tips
50 mm, at the midpoint of the flange
0 mm, exactly on the web midline
sol: Flange shear force F = ½·37.5·100 = 1875 N
Moment balance: V·e = F·h, e = 1875·200/1e4 = 37.5 mm

problems.x: The flange shear flows form a couple, so the channel's shear centre lies outside the section on the web's open back.

problems.title: Closed versus slit tube in torsion
problems.setup: A thin circular aluminum tube has mean radius R = 50 mm, wall t = 2 mm, length L = 1 m and G = 27 GPa. It carries a torque T = 1 kN·m. A second, identical tube has a full length longitudinal slit, making it an open section.

parts.ask: Shear stress in the closed tube
sol: Bredt: q = T/(2A), A = πR² = 7854 mm²

parts.ask: Twist of the closed tube over its length
Ratio of torsion constants J_closed/J_open
Explain why the slit tube is so much weaker in torsion.
parts.a: The closed tube carries torque by a constant shear flow circulating around the enclosed area, a lever arm of order R. The slit tube carries torque only by shear stress varying through the thickness, a lever arm of order t, so its stiffness scales with t³.
sol: Closed: torque via q around enclosed area 2A
Open: torque via through thickness stress gradient, J ∝ bt³
Stress ratio for equal torque is 3R/t = 75

problems.x: Closing a thin section lets the shear flow act over the enclosed area, multiplying torsional stiffness by about 3(R/t)².

problems.title: Castigliano on a loaded cantilever
problems.setup: A cantilever of length L = 2 m and EI = 4 MN·m² is clamped at x = 0. It carries a downward tip load P = 6 kN and a downward uniform load w = 3 kN/m over its full length. Use bending energy only; deflection is positive downward.

parts.ask: Which expression gives the tip deflection by Castigliano's second theorem?
sol: Write U = ∫ M²/(2EI) dx with P kept as a symbol at the point and direction of δ

parts.ask: Tip deflection
sol: With ξ = distance from the tip: M = Pξ + wξ²/2, ∂M/∂P = ξ

parts.ask: Tip rotation (add a dummy moment M₀ at the tip, then set M₀ = 0)
Doubling both loads changes the tip deflection by a factor of:
sol: For a linear elastic beam δ is linear in the loads
U is quadratic in the loads, and δ = ∂U/∂P is linear

problems.x: Castigliano gives any displacement as ∂U/∂(force at that point and direction), with a dummy load supplying the force when none is applied.

problems.title: Ritz on a spring supported beam
problems.setup: A simply supported beam of span L = 2 m and EI = 100 kN·m² rests on a linear spring k = 600 kN/m at midspan and carries a downward point load P = 12 kN at midspan. Use the one term trial function w(x) = a sin(πx/L), which satisfies the geometric boundary conditions.

parts.ask: Total potential energy Π(a) for this trial function:
sol: U_b = ½∫EI(w″)² dx = ½EI a²(π/L)⁴·L/2 = EIπ⁴a²/(4L³)
Spring energy ½k w(L/2)² = ½ka², load potential −P·a

parts.ask: Generalized beam stiffness EIπ⁴/(2L³)
Midspan deflection a
Force carried by the spring
sol: = 5.96 kN; the beam carries the remaining 6.04 kN

problems.x: Rayleigh-Ritz with admissible trial functions gives an upper bound on stiffness, so the Ritz deflection (9.93 mm) sits just below the exact 10 mm.

problems.title: Rigid bar: spring choice sets the post-buckling path
problems.setup: A rigid vertical bar of length L = 2 m is pinned at its base, restrained by a rotational spring k = 50 kN·m/rad, and carries a vertical dead load P at its top. Rotation θ is measured from vertical. Later the rotational spring is replaced by a horizontal translational spring k_t at the top that stays horizontal.

parts.ask: Critical load with the rotational spring
sol: d²Π/dθ² at θ = 0: k − PL = 0 ⇒ P_cr = k/L = 50/2 = 25 kN

parts.ask: Load on the post-buckling path at θ = 20°
sol: Equilibrium: kθ = PL sin θ ⇒ P = (k/L)·θ/sin θ

parts.ask: With the translational spring k_t = 12.5 kN/m, the critical load and post-buckling path are:
parts.a: P_cr = 25 kN, P = P_cr cos θ (unstable symmetric)
w: P_cr = 25 kN, P = P_cr θ/sin θ (stable symmetric)
P_cr = 6.25 kN, P = P_cr cos θ (unstable symmetric)
sol: Π = ½k_t L² sin²θ − PL(1 − cos θ)
dΠ/dθ = 0 ⇒ P = k_t L cos θ, so P_cr = 12.5·2 = 25 kN
P falls with |θ|: unstable symmetric bifurcation

parts.ask: Which of the two systems is imperfection sensitive, and why does it matter for design?
parts.a: The translational spring system is imperfection sensitive: its post-buckling load falls, so a small initial tilt gives a limit load below P_cr. The rotational spring system has a rising path, so an imperfect bar keeps carrying more load as it tilts and passes P_cr at finite tilt.
sol: Falling path ⇒ limit point below P_cr
Rising path ⇒ safe, stable symmetric bifurcation
Design knockdown factors apply to the unstable case

problems.x: The curvature of the post-buckling path (rising or falling) decides whether imperfections lower the load capacity below P_cr.

problems.title: Two DOF column with unequal springs
problems.setup: Two rigid links, each of length L = 0.5 m, are stacked vertically. A rotational spring 2k ties the bottom link to the ground and a rotational spring k joins the two links, with k = 20 kN·m/rad. A vertical dead load P acts at the free top. Use absolute link rotations θ₁ (bottom) and θ₂ (top) and small angle energy.

parts.ask: Stability matrix K (Hessian of Π about the straight state):
sol: K₁₁ = 3k − PL, K₁₂ = −k, K₂₂ = k − PL

parts.ask: Critical load P_cr
First mode ratio θ₂/θ₁
Second mode ratio θ₂/θ₁ (second root PL/k = 2 + √2)
sol: = −0.414: the links rotate in opposite senses

problems.x: The critical load is the smallest root of det K = 0, and its null vector gives the buckling mode.

problems.title: Propped cantilever with a central load
problems.setup: A beam of span L = 4 m is clamped at A (x = 0) and simply supported on a prop at B (x = L). It carries a downward point load P = 32 kN at midspan; EI is constant. Take the prop reaction R as the redundant.

parts.ask: Prop reaction R
sol: Released cantilever tip deflection from P: P(L/2)³/(3EI) + P(L/2)²/(2EI)·(L/2) = 5PL³/(48EI)
Prop: RL³/(3EI); compatibility gives R = 5P/16 = 10 kN

parts.ask: Magnitude of the fixed end moment at A
Sagging moment under the load
sol: Free body from B to midspan: M = R·L/2

parts.ask: The largest bending moment magnitude in the beam occurs at:
sol: |M_A| = 24 kN·m exceeds the 20 kN·m sagging moment under the load
The prop carries zero moment as a pin

problems.x: One compatibility equation at the released redundant (zero deflection at the prop) fixes all reactions of a once indeterminate beam.

problems.title: Strut braced wing as a beam on a spring
problems.setup: Model a strut braced wing as a cantilever of length L = 4 m, EI = 2 MN·m², clamped at the root and carrying an upward lift load w = 6 kN/m. A strut from the lower fuselage meets the wing tip at 30° to the wing; the strut's axial stiffness is EA/L_s = 1.125 MN/m. Neglect the wing's axial shortening.

parts.ask: Equivalent vertical stiffness of the strut at the tip
sol: A vertical tip motion v stretches the strut by v sin α

parts.ask: Vertical force R exerted by the strut on the tip (k_beam = 3EI/L³ = 93.75 kN/m)
sol: Free tip deflection δ_w = wL⁴/(8EI) = 6000·256/16e6 = 96 mm

parts.ask: Axial force in the strut (R = 6.75 kN)
sol: F = 6.75/0.5 = 13.5 kN, tension under upward lift

parts.ask: Root bending moment (R = 6.75 kN)

problems.x: A flexible support acts as a spring in series with the beam's own tip stiffness, and the rigid prop value 3wL/8 = 9 kN is its upper limit.

problems.title: Quarter ring: horizontal deflection and rotation
problems.setup: A thin quarter circle bar of radius R = 500 mm, centre O, is clamped at B, directly above O, so the arc rises from A to B. Its free end A lies on the horizontal radius. A downward vertical load P = 2 kN acts at A. EI = 5×10⁹ N·mm²; use bending energy only, with θ measured from OA so M(θ) = PR(1 − cos θ).

parts.ask: Vertical deflection of A (δ_v = (3π/4 − 2)PR³/EI)
Magnitude of the horizontal deflection of A (dummy horizontal load Q at A)
sol: Dummy moment m(θ) = R sin θ
δ_h = (PR³/EI)∫₀^{π/2}(1 − cos θ) sin θ dθ = (PR³/EI)(1 − ½)

parts.ask: Direction of the horizontal motion of A:
w: Away from the vertical radius OB
sol: Take Q at A pointing away from OB: its moment R sin θ has the opposite sense to PR(1 − cos θ)
So δ along Q equals −PR³/(2EI): A moves down and toward OB

parts.ask: Rotation of the tip A (dummy moment at A)

problems.x: Each displacement component of a curved bar comes from its own dummy load placed at the point and in the direction of interest.

problems.title: Steel plated timber beam
problems.setup: A timber beam 100 mm wide × 200 mm deep (E_t = 10 GPa) has a steel plate 100 mm wide × 10 mm thick (E_s = 200 GPa) perfectly bonded to its underside. It carries a sagging moment M = 20 kN·m. Use the transformed section in timber; y is measured up from the bottom of the steel.

parts.ask: Height of the neutral axis above the bottom of the steel
sol: n = E_s/E_t = 20, steel widened to 2000 mm: A = 20000 mm² at y = 5

parts.ask: Transformed second moment, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴
Compressive stress at the top of the timber
Tensile stress at the bottom of the steel

problems.x: Strain stays linear through a bonded section, so steel stress equals n times the transformed section stress at that depth.

problems.title: Effective length and the Johnson transition
problems.setup: A solid steel rod of diameter 40 mm (E = 200 GPa, σ_y = 350 MPa, radius of gyration r = d/4 = 10 mm) has length L = 1.5 m. First it stands as a flagpole: clamped at the base and free at the top. Then the same rod is installed clamped at both ends.

parts.ask: Euler load of the clamped free rod
sol: Clamped free: L_e = 2L = 3000 mm, I = πd⁴/64 = 125664 mm⁴

parts.ask: Transition slenderness between the Johnson parabola and Euler
Critical load of the clamped clamped rod by the Johnson parabola
Why is Johnson used for the clamped clamped case?
w: Johnson applies to every column with fixed ends
Euler applies only to free ends
sol: At this slenderness the column yields inelastically, which the Johnson parabola captures

problems.x: Effective length sets the slenderness, and slenderness below √(2π²E/σ_y) puts the column in the inelastic Johnson range.

problems.title: Bowed column amplification
problems.setup: A pinned pinned steel bar of square section 50 mm × 50 mm, length L = 2.5 m and E = 200 GPa has an initial half sine bow with midspan amplitude w₀ = 2.5 mm. It carries an axial compressive load P = 0.6 P_cr.

parts.ask: Euler load P_cr
Total midspan deflection under P = 0.6 P_cr
Maximum compressive stress at midspan (P = 98.7 kN, w = 6.25 mm)
As P approaches P_cr, the imperfect column:
parts.a: Deflection grows without bound as P → P_cr
w: Snaps through at about half of P_cr
Returns to the initial bow amplitude w₀ at every load
Reaches a peak load well above P_cr
sol: w_total = w₀/(1 − P/P_cr) grows as P/P_cr → 1
The stable symmetric Euler path makes P_cr the asymptote

problems.x: An initial bow is amplified by 1/(1 − P/P_cr), so bending stress grows rapidly well before the Euler load.
